content_metadata.description: An educational video exploring projectile motion in the context of the Apollo mission, focusing on comparing the projectile motion on the Moon to that on Earth.

qAndA.question: What is the initial velocity of the object in the problem?

qAndA.answer: The acceleration due to gravity on the moon (gₘ) is 1/6th of the acceleration due to gravity on Earth (gₑ).
qAndA.question: How does the acceleration due to gravity on the moon compare to that on Earth?
What is the angle at which the object is launched?

qAndA.answer: The range on the moon (rₘ) is greater than the range on Earth (rₑ) due to the lower gravity.
qAndA.question: How is the range of the projectile affected by the lower gravity on the moon?

qAndA.answer: Keeping variables in the equation until the end helps to minimize errors and provides a more elegant and traceable solution.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of keeping variables in the equation until the very end?

activities.description: Introduction to continuing the Apollo problem.
Explaining the derivation of the range formula and setting up the equation for comparing the range on the moon and Earth.
Simplifying the equation and plugging in values for the acceleration due to gravity on the moon and Earth.
Calculating the difference in time the ball is in the air on the moon compared to Earth.
Concluding remarks and summarizing the solution.

youtube_description:
This problem is divided in two. Please check 3.7.1 for the previous part. 

On the Apollo 14 mission to the moon, back in the day, astronaut Alan Shepard hit a golf ball with a 6 iron. The free-fall acceleration on the moon is 1/6 of its value on earth. Suppose he hit the ball with a speed of 25 m/s at an angle 30° above the horizontal.

1. How much farther did the ball travel on the moon than it would have on earth? The answer is 276 meters.

 2. For how much more time was the ball in flight? The answer is 12.75 seconds.
